title.title: Lipschitz maps from Hilbert space into $\ell_1$ extend
title.subtitle: Claim: $\ell_1$ has metric Markov cotype 2, with $N_2(\ell_1) \le 12\sqrt{21}$, which answers Ball's extension problem

plain: A stretch-limited map from part of a space into city-block distances can be extended to the whole space

beats.text: Ball (1992): Lipschitz maps extend into targets with Markov cotype 2
$\ell_1$ fails the linear version. The proof smooths each cut with this cubic
Claim: $\ell_1$ has the metric version, so maps from Hilbert space into $\ell_1$ extend

steps: Write city-block points as weighted cuts: vectors of 0s and 1s
Average them along a randomly stopped walk
Round with a cubic that is flat at 0 and 1, then map back

achievement.label: Mendel–Naor Question 1.15 (2013); Ball's extension problem
statement: f: A \subset H \to \ell_1 \text{ Lipschitz} \Rightarrow f \text{ extends to } H
achievement.context: Before: $\ell_1$ fails Ball's linear Markov cotype, so his theorem did not apply
achievement.note: Nine pages, dated the day before release; the extension step is quoted

verify.detail: No Lean. Short and elementary enough that an expert could check it in an afternoon
verify.ourCheck: We did not check the proof

voice.text: Ball reduced extending Lipschitz maps to two random walk inequalities. L one was open.
Write points as cuts, average along a walk, round with a cubic.
Claimed: L one has Markov cotype two.

sources.quote: Real l1 has metric Markov cotype two in the Mendel-Naor sense, with N_2(l1) <= 12 sqrt(21)
Ball (GAFA 2, 1992) introduced Markov type/cotype and proved his extension theorem (Markov type 2 source, Markov cotype 2 target); l1 fails Ball's linear Markov cotype.
